subject: Chemistry
description: Noble (inert) gases — Group 18, He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; properties, electron configuration, uses, history, key compounds.

questions.stem: Noble gases are also called INERT gases because they:

options.option_text: Have stable filled outer electron shells
React only with the alkali metals
Are radioactive in their natural state
Exist as solid metals at room temp

questions.explanation: NOBLE GASES (Group 18 / Group 0): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn. CHEMICALLY INERT (mostly) because they have FULL OUTER ELECTRON SHELLS — electron configuration ends in ns² np⁶ (except He = 1s²). Full octet means MAXIMUM STABILITY; no tendency to gain or lose electrons → no chemical reactions in normal conditions. EXCEPTIONS: starting in 1962, Neil Bartlett showed XENON forms compounds with very electronegative elements (XePtF₆); since then dozens of Xe and Kr compounds synthesized (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeO₄). Helium, Neon, Argon STILL essentially unreactive. PROPERTIES: (1) Colorless, odorless, tasteless gases. (2) Monatomic (single atoms, not molecules). (3) Low boiling points: He = 4.2 K (lowest of any element); Ne = 27 K; Ar = 87 K; Kr = 120 K; Xe = 165 K; Rn = 211 K. (4) Increasing density down the group (He lighter than air; Rn ~7× denser than air). DISCOVERY: ARGON (1894, Lord Rayleigh + William Ramsay — Nobel 1904); HELIUM detected in sun's spectrum (1868) before being isolated on Earth; Ne, Kr, Xe (1898 by Ramsay). RADON (1900) — radioactive. PYQ FREQUENCY: noble gas inertness in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which noble gas is used to fill BALLOONS and AIRSHIPS?
questions.explanation: HELIUM (He, atomic no. 2) — used to fill balloons because it's: (1) LIGHTER THAN AIR (density 0.18 g/L vs air's 1.29 g/L; ~7× less dense). (2) NON-FLAMMABLE (unlike hydrogen which is even lighter but explodes — Hindenburg disaster, 1937 — 36 deaths; ended commercial hydrogen-airship era). (3) COLORLESS, ODORLESS, NON-TOXIC. APPLICATIONS: (1) BALLOONS — party balloons, weather balloons, rescue balloons. (2) BLIMPS / AIRSHIPS — Goodyear blimp etc. use He. (3) MRI MACHINES — liquid helium (4.2 K) cools superconducting magnets. (4) DEEP-SEA DIVING — He-O₂ 'heliox' breathing mix avoids nitrogen narcosis. (5) WELDING shielding gas (with Ar). (6) SEMICONDUCTOR manufacturing. (7) LEAK DETECTION (small atom, escapes through tiny holes). HELIUM SHORTAGE: He is FINITE on Earth — collected from natural gas wells (where helium accumulates from radioactive decay). U.S. Federal Helium Reserve was main source. Modern shortage threatens MRI/research. SOLUTIONS: capture during natural gas processing; some new producers in Qatar, Russia. INDIA imports almost all helium. ON THE SUN: helium is the SECOND most abundant element (after hydrogen), ~24% of stellar mass. NAME: from 'helios' (Greek for sun). PYQ FREQUENCY: helium uses in NEET, NCERT, SSC chemistry 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which noble gas is commonly used in NEON SIGN BOARDS, glowing red?
questions.explanation: NEON (Ne) — when an electric current passes through low-pressure neon gas in a sealed glass tube, it emits a CHARACTERISTIC ORANGE-RED GLOW. Used in NEON SIGNS (Las Vegas, Tokyo, etc.) — the term 'neon sign' is now generic, but ORIGINAL neon glows red. OTHER COLORS in 'neon' signs use different gases: (1) ARGON — pale BLUE/VIOLET. (2) HELIUM — pale yellowish-pink. (3) KRYPTON — yellow-greenish white. (4) XENON — bluish-white. (5) MERCURY VAPOR — bright blue (in fluorescent tubes; UV exciting phosphor coating gives white light). (6) NEON + MERCURY + Phosphor combinations — full color range. INDIA NEON SIGNS: bustling around Mumbai, Bengaluru tech hubs, Connaught Place Delhi. NAME: 'NEON' from 'neos' (Greek for 'new'). DISCOVERED 1898 by William Ramsay + Morris Travers in London. CURRENT TRENDS: traditional neon being replaced by LED-based 'neon-flex' for energy efficiency, longevity, lower maintenance. NEON's CHEMISTRY: most inert of the noble gases — even Bartlett-style xenon compounds don't readily form for neon. INDUSTRIAL USES: (1) Helium-Neon (HeNe) lasers — common red laser pointers (633 nm). (2) Neon vacuum tubes for indicators in electronic equipment. PYQ FREQUENCY: neon-orange glow is a SSC GA, NEET classic 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which noble gas is filled in INCANDESCENT bulbs to extend filament life?
questions.explanation: ARGON (Ar) — most common gas filled in INCANDESCENT BULBS. WHY: (1) INERT — won't react with hot tungsten filament (which would oxidize/burn out in air). (2) Heavier than helium/neon → BETTER at suppressing tungsten evaporation from filament (extends life). (3) Cheap — Argon is ~1% of Earth's atmosphere; obtained by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION of LIQUID AIR. (4) Doesn't conduct heat well → keeps filament hot. TYPICAL FILL: 90% Argon + 10% Nitrogen. HALOGEN BULBS use halogens (iodine, bromine) + Ar — halogen gas reacts with evaporated tungsten and redeposits it on filament (HALOGEN CYCLE) — much longer life, brighter. KRYPTON (Kr) — used in some HIGH-PERFORMANCE bulbs (better filament protection but more expensive). USE in OTHER APPLICATIONS: (1) WELDING — argon shielding gas (prevents oxidation of weld). (2) DOUBLE-PANE WINDOWS — Ar between panes for insulation. (3) FOOD PACKAGING — flushing oxygen out (extends shelf life). (4) WINE PRESERVATION (replaces oxygen above wine in opened bottle). (5) Lab inert atmosphere for sensitive chemistry. ABUNDANCE: Ar is the THIRD most abundant gas in atmosphere (~0.93%, after N₂ and O₂); produced industrially as byproduct of liquid-air distillation (millions of tonnes/year). PYQ FREQUENCY: argon uses in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: RADON (Rn), a noble gas, is significant because it is:
questions.explanation: RADON (Rn, atomic no. 86) — the only RADIOACTIVE noble gas. Half-life ~3.8 days (Rn-222, the most stable isotope). Comes from URANIUM-238 decay chain in soil/rock; seeps into homes through cracks, well water. HEALTH HAZARD: SECOND LEADING CAUSE OF LUNG CANCER (after smoking). Inhaled radon decays in lungs; alpha particles damage tissue. Globally ~3-14% of lung cancers attributed to radon. INDIA — not as severe as USA/Europe (less granitic geology in residential areas). USA has comprehensive radon-mitigation programs (vent fans under basements). DISCOVERY: 1900 by Friedrich Ernst Dorn (Germany). ALL RADON ISOTOPES are radioactive — no stable form. ABUNDANCE: in air ~10⁻¹⁹% (extremely rare). USES: (1) RADIATION THERAPY (some old cancer treatments — now mostly replaced). (2) GEOLOGICAL — radon levels predict earthquakes, locate uranium deposits. RADON DAUGHTERS: decays into Polonium-218, Lead-214, etc. — the alpha-emitters that lodge in lungs and cause damage. SAFETY MEASURES: radon detection kits available; ventilation; sealing basement cracks. ANALOG: PURE NOBLE GASES are mostly safe; only HEAVIEST (Rn) is hazardous due to radioactivity. PYQ FREQUENCY: radon-radioactivity in NEET, NCERT, UPSC environment 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which noble gas is used in HIGH-INTENSITY arc lamps (like in cinema projectors and car headlamps)?
questions.explanation: XENON (Xe, atomic no. 54) — used in HIGH-INTENSITY DISCHARGE (HID) arc lamps because: (1) Produces VERY BRIGHT WHITE-BLUE LIGHT (close to natural daylight). (2) HIGH efficacy + good color rendering. (3) Stable arc, long life. APPLICATIONS: (1) CINEMA PROJECTORS — XENON SHORT-ARC LAMPS — power 1-15 kW; produce immense brightness needed for huge screens. (2) CAR HEADLAMPS (HID 'XENON' headlights) — much brighter than halogen, longer-life. (3) STROBE LIGHTS / FLASH LAMPS for photography (xenon flash tubes — short bursts, ~1/1000 sec). (4) IMAX projectors (high-power xenon). (5) SEARCHLIGHTS / lighthouse lamps. (6) UV light therapy (some skin treatments). KEY ADVANTAGES: (a) DIMMABLE, can be cycled. (b) Doesn't contain mercury (unlike fluorescent lamps). (c) Extremely high luminous output. CHEMISTRY MILESTONE: in 1962, Neil Bartlett synthesized XePtF₆ — FIRST stable noble gas COMPOUND, shattering the 'inert' label. Now Xe and Kr are known to form many compounds: XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeOF₄, XeO₄, even XeCl₂ (transient). DISCOVERED: 1898 by Ramsay + Travers. RECENT: xenon is also studied as a future ANESTHETIC gas (very potent + safe but expensive). PYQ FREQUENCY: xenon uses in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: ELECTRON CONFIGURATION ending in ns²np⁶ is characteristic of which group?
questions.explanation: GROUP 18 (NOBLE GASES) have FULL OUTER SHELLS: ns² np⁶ (8 outer electrons, octet). EXCEPTION: HELIUM has only 1s² (2 electrons; n=1 only has s subshell, no p subshell). FULL CONFIGURATIONS (memorize): (1) HELIUM: 1s². (2) NEON: [He] 2s² 2p⁶. (3) ARGON: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶. (4) KRYPTON: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶. (5) XENON: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁶. (6) RADON: [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶. RELATED CONFIGURATIONS by group: GROUP 1 (alkali metals, Li, Na, K): ns¹ — one outer electron; very reactive (lose e⁻ to form +1 ion). GROUP 2 (alkaline earth, Be, Mg, Ca): ns². GROUP 17 (halogens, F, Cl, Br): ns² np⁵ — one less than octet, very reactive (gain e⁻ to form −1 ion). GROUP 16 (chalcogens, O, S, Se): ns² np⁴. KEY: noble gases are TARGETS — when other elements REACT, they often try to ACHIEVE noble-gas configuration by gaining/losing electrons (OCTET RULE). PERIODIC TRENDS in NOBLE GASES: (1) ATOMIC SIZE increases down (more shells). (2) Ionization energy DECREASES down. (3) Boiling/melting points INCREASE down (more London dispersion). PYQ FREQUENCY: noble gas e-config in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.
